When these disks collapse, they give rise to powerful jets that can emit gamma-rays. By incorporating the effect of general relativity and synthesizing data from various sources, a hypothetical example shows that gamma-ray emission from one galaxy could be attributed to a captured disk system rather than dark matter. Consequently, revising the estimated amount of dark matter in this galaxy is no longer necessary. The proposal merits further investigation, given the limited data available and the complexity of the underlying physics.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis can be impaired by background noise and movement-related distortion during the examination. To address this challenge, an automatic system for heart sound analysis is necessary. Such a system could help medical professionals quickly identify issues like heart valve problems by analyzing recordings from physical examinations. To develop an effective cardiac auscultation tool, researchers must consider how the system processes recordings with noise and distortion. To demonstrate the effectiveness of various heart sound classification systems in real-world applications, an investigative framework is needed. This paper evaluates the accuracy of existing methods as well as two proposed techniques for automatically diagnosing heart valve conditions. The first proposed technique combines features from signals affected by noise, while the second technique uses a convolutional neural network that is resistant to noise and distortion. Both techniques were tested using publicly available datasets of heart sound recordings with different levels of background noise and were found to be accurate systems for cardiac auscultation at different levels of precision.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. However, these devices usually identify their users and process a high volume of data that makes it difficult to ensure privacy protection. In order to address this issue, a privacy-preserving framework called FedHealth has been proposed for training machine learning models on inertial sensor data within a federated transfer learning framework. This framework enables effective, robust healthcare services while protecting user privacy. A study using inertial sensor data for fall detection showed that FedHealth's performance was comparable to a traditional machine learning model, and it had a notable advantage when trained on a smaller dataset, outperforming the standard model by 13%.

This study explores potential connections between portfolio optimization methods that account for higher-order moments, including skewness and kurtosis. When combining portfolios that are optimized for mean-variance and semi-deviation measures, we observe a intriguing relationship that can be explained by a quadratic equation. By contrast, when combining portfolios optimized for semi-deviation and excess kurtosis, the relationship is more complex and varies depending on the relative weights of the underlying normal distribution and asymmetric heavy-tailed components. We propose several theoretical models to better understand these relationships, and in the process, several known methods can be seen as special cases of a more general framework.

In large-scale automation environments, software often needs to be configured
and run manually, taking precious time and causing obstacles for developers.
For example, in cloud-based testing, software must be started on each individual
machine before tests can be conducted, consuming significant time and effort.
Additionally, in robotic arms' simulation-based programming, software must be
compiled and run on each link before defining their motion, leading to similar
frustrations.
This paper introduces a novel concept called "Automated Software Handling" to address these issues, involving the creation of specialized, easily shareable
"software cartridges" that can be instantly loaded onto systems, allowing software
to operate automatically without compilation or other manual interventions.

This research focuses on a stochastic control problem where the objective function to minimize includes the number of times the control switches, making it a version of a problem with switching costs. Unlike traditional variants, we do not assume costs are paid at the exact points of switching, but rather there is a time interval required for the control to switch. This results in the problem having natural hurdles at the points of switching, in addition to boundary conditions at the extremes of the state space. We establish the existence of an optimal strategy and demonstrate that, under certain conditions, it is possible to find a solution by using a variety of approximation methods, including the value function's characterization as the infimum of values to systems with constraints, and the PDE it satisfies, as well as the possibility of solving it as an embedded problem with costs paid at the points of switching.

To explore the potential origins of recent anomalous observations in high-energy particle collisions, a theoretical analysis suggests creating two specific types of unusual particles known as leptoquarks through a single high-energy proton-proton collision. This study examines how even or odd (in pairs) these two particles are created, depending on the underlying physics driving the process. Even pairs would result from specific underlying processes, whereas odd pairs could stem from a variety of processes. By comparing the patterns of leptoquark creation, even or odd, this study aims to help identify the underlying physics and reconcile the results with existing experiments, all within the framework of a well-established theoretical framework that combines elements of high-energy particle collisions and unusual matter properties.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found that even at the outer reaches of galaxies, the gas is often warmer than expected, sometimes by factors of ten. This unexpected warmth could be causing problems for the theory of star formation, which is based on the idea that molecules must first be heated by stars before they can form new galaxies. To better understand this issue, we are going to look at how warm the gas is in a sample of small galaxies that are far from any star formation.

We address the series reconstruction problem for permutations, which is a key issue arising in statistical applications, including genetics and network analysis. In these contexts, representing data as intricate patterns of rearranged elements can lead to more precise modeling, but doing so requires estimating the underlying order, a challenge that, as the number of data points increases, becomes increasingly difficult using traditional methods. We introduce a novel approach that utilizes the Hamming distance and leverages partial information to estimate the order of a permutation, and we outline an iterative algorithm to accomplish this. Moreover, we discuss an alternative method using a divergence-based approach and review an associated theoretical guarantee. These techniques can be applied to various statistical analyses, including testing the equality of distributions, constructing confidence regions for the order of a permutation, and implementing multiple model selection procedures.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual binary black hole mergers in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing the computational time for different methods, our study demonstrates how the accuracy of PTA signal models can be significantly improved while significantly reducing the computational expense. Specifically, we show that using a simple approximate model, rather than a more precise one, can lead to a $10^4$ times reduction in computational time, allowing for much higher precision in detections. Furthermore, we provide an publicly accessible code for modeling such signals and demonstrate the efficacy of searching for these signals using a matched filter in a mock PTA dataset.

We illustrate how the ASEP random velocity model serves as a natural framework for studying various discrete transport equations, including non-Newtonian diffusion, fractional diffusion, and the Burgers equation, through a velocity aggregation process. We examine initial data with growing moments to exhibit how the ASEP velocity model's characteristics evolve over time, and we derive precise upper and lower bounds on the velocity fluctuations' second moments using Green function techniques. Additionally, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the velocity distribution's variance, finding that it follows a particular power law for a wide range of time steps, and we provide a more rigorous analysis for the special case of second-class exclusion model with the hydrodynamic scaling time step.

Our analysis compares and contrasts different mathematical models being used to study the COVID-19 pandemic, including detailed discussions of epidemic models, asymptomatic infection models, multi-group models, super-spreader events models, travel-related infection models, vaccine evaluation models, and models for predicting healthcare systems' capacity and critical breakdown points. Although there are variations, most models share common frameworks that incorporate key elements such as contact rates, infection probabilities, asymptotic characteristics, and various response measures implemented by individuals and society. Our examination highlights the importance of choosing an appropriate model framework based on available data and the specific question being addressed.

We have theoretically analyzed a novel phenomenon called particle-molecule transformation, which occurs when a spin-1 particle interacts with a spinless laser field and multiple particles are created. This transformation can take various forms, depending on the specific conditions, and we have examined three scenarios: particle-molecule conversion, demagnetization, and themagneto-optical trapping. This process is inversely similar to three-body recombination, where two interacting particles result in a bound state and excess energy, and it involves competing processes that affect average distances between interacting particles and the characteristics of bound states. This phenomenon could potentially be experimented with using cold atoms, and would provide new insights into many-body physics.

This paper proposes an improved DNA storage technology that enhances the efficiency of data hierarchy and update operations. Initially, we illustrate how to create a hierarchical representation of data utilizing fixed-length binary words, which allows for precise identification of specific data segments based on their positions. We then develop a dual-encoded system for updating frequency-based binary codes representing numerical data. This dual-encoded approach ensures the validity of updated codes and provides a way to track changes made to the original codes. We also explore the possibility of combining encoded updates into existing storage channels. Our proposed storage technology and update methods can be utilized together to create an efficient and hierarchical data storage system. Additionally, we outline the feasibility of our proposed architecture and estimated costs of implementation based on current DNA sequencing and synthesis prices. Our data hierarchy representation and frequency-based encoding can result in storage savings of 89% and 84%, respectively. We estimate that our storage technology could support up to 1 GByte of stored data, and we outline the potential performance gains achievable with this storage technology.

The precise prediction of ocean flows is crucial for identifying submerged objects and ensuring safe navigation. Traditional methods for predicting these flows using the shallow water equations are time-consuming and inefficient, necessitating faster alternatives. A novel approach has been developed where the shallow water equations are reconfigured to produce a single stream function value, enabling the recovery of multiple flow variables with accuracy. This method, known as the source distribution method, leverages source distribution and boundary integral representations to efficiently solve the shallow water equations. It has been proven effective in modeling various ocean flows, including complex scenarios with multiple obstacles and moving objects. By validating this method against established solutions and real-world data, a reliable and fast scheme has been established for predicting underwater objects from flow simulations.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a novel technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone images by leveraging the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative method called weighted fusion is introduced to combine images captured at different exposure levels. This technique utilizes the sensitivity of each pixel to drive the fusion process, resulting in sharper and more detailed HDR images. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial for smartphones with limited RAW image capabilities, allowing for high-quality HDR images to be created directly on the device. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the proposed technique's effectiveness in capturing high-quality HDR images, even in challenging lighting situations.

In this talk, we examine the fundamental principles underlying how neural networks, specifically those with linear inputs and logistic outputs, learn from random data. Building on recent findings (Goldberg et al., 2020; Saldana et al., 2020; Gueijbel et al., 2020; Baraniuk et al., 2020; Gueijbel et al., 2021; Saldana et al., 2021; Baraniuk et al., 2021; Saldana et al., 2022; Gueijbel et al., 2022; Saldana et al., 2023; Baraniuk et al., 2023; Saldana et al., 2023), we explore how the structure of these networks influences their ability to distinguish relevant features from irrelevant ones, especially in high-dimensional spaces.

This note presents a new category of map functions called oriented map functions, which includes oriented bundle map functions as a subset. Building on the research of Madsen-McGaugh, it is proven that in certain cases, oriented map functions are stable under a specific type of variation, known as homotopy equivalences, if they are true embeddings. This phenomenon is seen as significant because oriented map functions can be viewed as a variation of the original statement of the b-principle, also known as the basic principle, which is a fundamental concept in category theory with applications in various fields, including topology, geometry, and computer science. This result is particularly notable among researchers in the field of algebraic geometry, as it solves a long-standing problem known as the Mumford conjecture and provides a key component in proving the stability of a specific geometric feature known as intersection numbers under variations.

This study compares the efficiency of various multilevel numerical methods for solving cardiac mechanics problems by means of nonlinear partial differential equations. A specific approach based on a combination of finite elements and lattice differential equations has been examined as an alternative to conventional methods. A detailed analysis of a previous study [12] on this topic is given, along with new findings for both thin films and comprehensive heart models. A discussion on recent optimizations [21,28] and another approach [25] involving lattice finite differences is also provided.

We investigate a novel model of random permeability changes, which drives a stochastic diffusion process and causes it to experience both lateral diffusion and vertical sub-diffusion. This process is governed by a fractional Laplace operator and represents a more realistic representation of physical processes than traditional fractional diffusion models. This new model can be seen as a variation of recent ideas presented in other research, however our approach uses a different mathematical formulation. This process can be interpreted through the lens of geometric construction, using random permeability scenarios, and it reflects the physical principles of porous media. We then develop a comprehensive framework for solving a related convection-diffusion problem, and obtain a number of notable results, including the existence and characterization of solutions, as well as the asymptotic behavior of associated moments. This involves applying sophisticated mathematical tools, such as Banach space-valued operators, embedded fractals, and embedded random fields.

A mode-interaction model is a necessary tool for understanding both linear and nonlinear phenomena in optical systems, and our enhanced framework builds upon the fundamental work of other researchers. We have expanded the previous approach to accommodate both waveguides and resonators and have demonstrated the mode-interaction model's capabilities by applying it to analyze both linear mode coupling and Kerr nonlinear phase modulation, with the option of a variable beam size.

A proposed new method utilizes GRNN and GAN models to enhance the resolution of turbulent flow images captured at various Reynolds numbers. The proposed technique involves creating a high-resolution simulation model based on a GAN and a low-resolution experimental model integrated through a GRNN, and then combining these models to achieve the desired high-resolution results. A representative case study involving the enhancement of a turbulent flow simulation at a Reynolds number of 460 is presented, and the method's effectiveness is measured by analyzing the obtained data.

For large language models like T0 and XLNet, evaluating training is a crucial step, representing a significant challenge. To effectively assess these models, we must consider multiple diverse evaluation metrics across various tasks, spanning classification, conversational, and machine translation. Furthermore, since large language models are infinitely trainable, we require an evaluation framework that can accommodate endless assessment scenarios. In response to these difficulties, we present L2Explorer, a comprehensive evaluation ecosystem designed to accommodate endless reinforcement learning evaluations. L2Explorer is characterized by six distinct features: it is limitless in scope, evaluates models based on multiple, varied tasks, includes both manual and automated configuration options, permits both centralized and decentralized management, incorporates both human-centric and machine-centric feedback, and provides both anonymous and attributed evaluation settings.

The automatic discovery of business processes relies on process discovery techniques, which can be triggered by continuous data streams. Our approach develops an algorithm that combines exploration and surveillance modes to identify declarative processes from data streams, taking into account variations in process behavior. The process is represented as a sound and complete language model, which is periodically refined during the exploration mode to ensure it accurately reflects the underlying process, while in the surveillance mode it is used to compare the observed data to expected process behavior. Our approach detects deviations in process behavior and provides actionable feedback in the form of recommendations to revise the process. We have tested the algorithm using real data streams and simulated processes, comparing its effectiveness to existing process discovery techniques, and found it to be on par with them in terms of process accuracy and variability detection.

This research focuses on the parameter space P of a given polynomial equation P. If P defines a rational surface, the paper demonstrates that both the algebraic model defined by the discriminant locus and the analytic model defined by the compactified space U_hboundarly converge to the same scheme within the algebraic framework. Conversely, if the algebraic and analytic compactifications of P result in the same scheme, we prove that P defines a rational surface with a specific, identifiable characteristic.

We investigated the relationship between maximum star formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass ($M_\omega$) in a database of 22,697 galaxies. We found that the existing break in the $M_\omega$-SFR ratio at $\log M_\omega \approx 10.2$ may be influenced by bulge dominance, as it is absent in galaxies with little or no central bulge. For galaxies with a distinguishing bulge, a second threshold at $\log M_\omega \approx 10.5$ is observed, above which the $M_\omega$-SFR ratio decreases. This could imply that massive bulges with low SFR levels inhibit star formation, contributing to the turning point in the $M_\omega$-SFR ratio at $\log M_\omega \approx 10.5$.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using a multi-lingual corpus. The study
focuses on four languages: English, Spanish, French, and Portuguese. To
achieve this, an automated approach was developed which combines the
word-to-vector translation technique of multilingual word embeddings with
the application of convolutional neural networks. The proposed framework was
tested on four languages and compared to a monolingual approach, showing a
significant improvement in accuracy. Furthermore, the model was applied to
multi-task learning, demonstrating enhanced performance for three of the four
languages. The evaluation also revealed an increase in overall sentiment
prediction accuracy through multi-task training. The code for this project is
publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with diagnostic and prognostic potential for COVID-19 patients, particularly those with severe symptoms requiring intensive care. To facilitate automated analysis of these images, their underlying features should be identified and described in a quantitative framework. This paper outlines a novel approach to extracting and categorizing essential properties from lung images using machine learning methods. A concise numerical code is introduced to represent both image content and object-based characteristics. This code can be further trained on classification algorithms to predict critical outcomes such as ICU admission. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a manual analysis of image features was performed for 25 COVID-19 patients, and a convolutional neural network was used to classify 10 patients likely to require intensive care. The results show that this approach can accurately identify patients who need intensive care with an accuracy of 80%.

Given a bundle X → B with structure map π, we construct the global simplicial bundle ΣX → ΣB, using the simplicial structure of the mapping space SimpN∗(X) → SimpN∗(B). We prove that the simplicial structure of the mapping space SimpN∗(X) → SimpN∗(B) is compatible with the bundle properties, specifically it is a bundle with respect to the simplicial index N. This shows that the simplicial structure is invariant under pre-composition, and the face maps ΔiN induce bundle morphisms ΔiN: ΣX → ΣB. Moreover, the degeneracy maps ΔjN: ΣX → ΣB are bundle submersions with respect to the simplicial index N.

The problem of erroneous positives in visual association detection persists, hindering the development of reliable and precise methods. Despite significant progress made by the current state-of-the-art in the field, achievable performance has yet to be defined. To address this challenge, the standard detection evaluation metric is being adapted to account for existing difficulties. Specifically, the weighted average of precision at different recall levels will be utilized as the primary evaluation metric. Additionally, an analysis of current limitations and potential obstacles to further improvement has been explored. These analysis reveal that existing datasets may no longer accurately reflect real-world challenges due to excessive ease, and that attention-based models may have reached a saturation point, requiring novel paradigms such as dual-training systems to achieve significant gains.

We've performed super-high resolution simulations of a young galaxy cluster for three hundred million years, modeling the interaction of multiple galaxies that have merged and dispersed. These simulations maintain a high level of detail, accurately representing the movement and collision of stars within each galaxy, even down to the level of individual star interactions. As a result, we've obtained highly realistic representations of collisionless gravitational interactions, mirroring the behavior of galaxies in actual galaxy clusters. These simulations have enabled us to develop a comprehensive understanding of a specific galaxy's development, specifically a disk galaxy that has experienced a major merger. According to our simulations, this galaxy experienced a significant buildup of bulge stars through the disruption of a star cluster by a high velocity dispersion, sparked by the initial merger. This resulted in the development of multiple well-defined star formation suppression regions, affecting both its central and outer regions. Notably, these regions played a crucial role in shaping its overall structure, particularly the development of its bulge and the disappearance of certain star formation regions in its outer areas. In the process, we've obtained useful insights into the complex relationships between bulge formation, star creation, and the disruption of star clusters, demonstrating how the interaction between different mass galaxies can give rise to varied bulge formations through the collisionless gravitational effects of gravity.

Recently discovered documents related to solar physics shed new light on an important event - the massive solar flare of November 7, 2004. During this event, extremely low frequency radio waves caused widespread interference, making it more challenging to accurately measure higher frequency observations. By reanalyzing data from the Solar Neutron Decomposition Protons experiment, researchers were able to better understand the effects of this flare on the Sun's upper atmosphere. Their findings reveal that the energy released resulted in the formation of unusual particle patterns, and they suggest that this phenomenon may have contributed to the diminished low frequency interference. Additionally, the documents reveal details about the technical issues encountered and solutions found to optimize the measurement of high frequency observations.

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of a notable phenomenon observed during the spin-up of KW Dor, an eccentric binary star. KW Dor's light curves display unusual patterns of shining brightly at both extremes of its orbital cycle, which has sparked hypotheses about the presence of a substantial amount of absorption caused by planetary objects or alternatively, unforeseen angular momentum transfer affecting its rotation.

Due to the rapid dissemination of information on social media, fake news can spread quickly, and detecting it has become an urgent task. Deep learning models have made significant progress in fake news detection, but most current approaches rely on large amounts of labeled data, making them less practical for everyday use. Additionally, recent adversarial attacks have led to a surge of interest in exploring emerging concepts in machine learning, whose benefits include boosting robustness against label manipulation and proxy tasks generalizing well to new instances. This paper proposes a novel framework called Multimodal Meta Neural Process for Counterfeit News Detection, integrating the strengths of both neural processes and meta-learning, to effectively handle the task of detecting counterfeit news. This model utilizes the relationship between training and testing data to provide accurate predictions on unknown classes, while the paper also explores the benefits of using synthetic counterfeit news to enhance real-world detection tasks. Experiments conducted on multiple dataset combinations demonstrate the proposed framework's superiority over existing methods, showcasing its potential for scaling to large datasets and robust performance in incremental learning.

This research paper examines a recurring transport equation with variables in two spaces and the effect of it having multiple solutions. The recurring framework is characterized by an iterative process that incorporates an operator A, a measure-defined operator B, and the operator ad with respect to the variable adu. The paper's main argument is that if the recurring transport equation has multiple solutions, then both operators B and adu must have multiple solutions to the corresponding equations, assuming certain conditions are met. Notably, this conclusion holds even if the space has no discontinuity requirements. The paper's recurrent framework can be applied to modeling certain economic systems and is therefore relevant to those studies.

A diverse array of designs that incorporate Golay complementary sequences in multiple phases has been explored. These diverse designs, structured around phase-based Golay complementary arrays, are distinguished by their complementary pairings across varying phases. It has been demonstrated that phase-defined Golay complementary sequences can be combined to form designs that employ up to four phases, encompassing both even and odd phase configurations. Even phase designs incorporate pairs of phase-defined Golay complementary sequences in each of the four phases, whereas odd phase designs integrate all four phases into a single complementary pair. Both even and odd phase designs meet the criteria for partial pairwise complementarity, allowing them to demonstrate enhanced autocorrelation and cross-correlation properties.

Quantum interactions between electronic valleys in silicon hold significant promise for building robust and efficient quantum processors. To capitalize on this potential, it's crucial to understand how valley states interact with electrons in impurity-based spin transfer protocols. This article examines valley state interaction in silicon, specifically with phosphorus impurities, which have a direct relationship with spin transfer and quantum processing units. However, previous studies underestimated the effect of valley interaction, describing it as negligible. Conversely, our findings indicate that valley interaction cannot be disregarded, particularly when protocol protocols involve high-frequency driving methods. Moreover, a shift in valley interaction was observed, which was attributed to a phenomenon known as valley polarization. This phenomenon affects electron distribution between valley states and compensates for mass differences through structural strain. Our approach involves combining methods of ab initio simulations, effective mass models, and drive-field valley polarization, which may be applied to various impurity-based systems beyond silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interconnected components typically follow nonlinear dynamics that can lead to devastating consequences due to the sudden failure of specific parts. To mitigate these effects, researchers focus on optimizing architecture and dynamics to obtain better performance and stability. Although effective, this process is often time-consuming due to limited access to precise dynamic models and extensive computational cost associated with modeling architecture. In our research, we propose a novel approach that leverages data alone to develop a stochastic graph neural network architecture and extracts valuable insights to optimize dynamics and architecture. By conducting experiments with multiple complex systems, including artificial examples and real-world models, we demonstrate our approach's ability to achieve significant performance improvements and robustness enhancements.

The study of mathematical structures through partition functions has been a valuable tool in understanding the behavior of complex systems. From the fundamental energies in physics, representing thermodynamic potentials, to the modular functions in number theory, describing the distribution of prime numbers, these functions reveal crucial insights into the underlying dynamics. In the realm of homotopy theory, Witten obtained the partition function related to the Rayson-Switzer extension of the Alexander-Singer relative cohomology, leveraging it to demonstrate the nontriviality of specific invariant constructs. Building upon this finding, the associated Verlinde algebra is explored in the context of this partition function, with implications for the classification of invariant constructs.

A cutting-edge healthcare challenge lies in the automatic detection and identification of cerebral lesions from MRI data, as many techniques require extensive manual input and have limited accuracy, especially for difficult cases, such as posterior fossa lesions, where atlas selection and registration are particularly difficult. To address this issue, a novel technique is proposed that leverages a sophisticated neural network framework called Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder, enabling the direct generation of personalized MRI images that include artificially created lesions, without the need for time-consuming and complicated atlas selection and registration processes. By deploying a complex network of 18 million parameters, consisting of multiple variational and adversarial components, the proposed technique significantly enhances the accuracy of lesion detection on newly generated images by up to 95%, and significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating superior performance in various evaluations.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the compilation process, the GP 2 compiler was upgraded to utilise a more advanced matching algorithm for rooted rules, leading to a significant reduction in compilation time. Additionally, the upgraded compiler optimises compiled programs to eliminate unnecessary safety restrictions, thereby preventing unnecessary slowing down of future program transformations. The benefits of the improved compiler are illustrated through a case study, where the compilation time for a specific program was found to be 12 times shorter than before.

In recent years, attribute extraction from text has gained significant interest, and a number of approaches have been explored to achieve this task using contrastive learning methods. Although significant progress has been observed, there is still room for improvement, especially when it comes to scaling up to large attribute sets. Currently, most techniques construct separate pairs for each attribute, leading to an explosion of pairs that need to be generated for large sets, and resulting in poor performance. In contrast, our proposed unified structure for attribute extraction stands out by creating a single pair that encompasses all attributes, enabling the model to distinguish between them automatically. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to both small and large attribute sets, obtaining state-of-the-art results on widely used benchmark datasets for text attribute extraction, including ATC, CTR, and WISER.

We have identified a new class of locally finite graph automorphisms that act on an infinite series of twisted wreath trees. These trees are not hamiltonian connected and their cycle length can be arbitrarily large. This provides counterexamples for specific graph-theoretical properties, including the assumption that hamiltonian connectivity is equivalent to cycle recognition and another involving the relationship between cycle recognition and infinite hedgehog properties.

Working with categorical data in model selection can be complicated due to the complex relationships between categories and the presence of multiple hypotheses. Typically, each categorical variable is treated as a group of equivalent features, but this approach ignores the inherent structure within the variables. For example, multiple levels of a category are often equivalent to polytomous outcomes. Nevertheless, these additional levels are often unnecessary and can result in overfitting. To address this challenge, a new Group Lasso variant is introduced, which allows for the inclusion of internal structure within categorical variables through separate feature selections. This new method is particularly effective for modeling relationships between categories and can significantly reduce model complexity without a separate feature design, making it particularly suitable for high-dimensional data.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance in various tasks, yet these models often excel at isolated issues but struggle with more complex, extensively described problems. In contrast, humans readily incorporate numerous details to solve intricate dilemmas. To bridge this gap, we develop a novel approach, combining structured insight into extensive text to enhance current large language models. By integrating this method, known as SKILL, into the T5 framework, we significantly improve the performance of our base model for math word problems by an average of 13.6%. Furthermore, SKILL demonstrates versatility in enhancing models for other complex tasks characterized by extensive background information.

Achieving a seamless visual experience with mapping applications requires the efficient display of lines on display devices. Since line connections are often displayed in the form of connected segments, there's a common practice of rendering adjacent segments close to each other. This rendering approach can cause adjacent segments to intersect incorrectly if the transformation from one segment to the next isn't calculated accurately. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel method for rendering line connections by utilizing a transformation function that considers the characteristics of line connections and devices. By utilizing this rendering method, line connections can be displayed correctly, even on devices with limited processing power. A subsequent experimental evaluation confirms that this rendering method maintains high performance while ensuring the correctness of line connections, and it outperforms the existing interpolation-based rendering method in terms of rendering accuracy and spatial anti-aliasing effectiveness.

For single-channel speech enhancement in noisy environments, a system with two outputs is desired - one for each microphone signal with minimal noise, and an integrated output representing the enhanced speech signal. To achieve this, we propose the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) architecture, comprising two separate networks working in tandem to adapt to different frequency domains. The first network filters noise in the low-frequency domain while the second network addresses the mid-to-high frequency domain. These networks are connected through a dual structure, allowing them to influence each other through bypass paths. The proposed DPCRN architecture outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various noisy scenario configurations, demonstrating its robustness in modeling frequency domain relationships.

Recently introduced multi-fluid modeling has promised to enhance the accuracy of atmospheric circulation modeling. A dynamic framework, which utilizes two fluids to represent air and moisture, underpins this approach. To further develop this method, researchers are conducting idealized simulations of atmospheric convection using this two-fluid model. The current study builds upon previous studies by utilizing more realistic temperature profiles and moisture contents in its simulations. A comprehensive analysis of the model's results under different two-fluid representation configurations is conducted to identify patterns of convection and moisture accumulation within the atmosphere. The findings of this research will serve as a foundation for exploring full-scale multi-fluid modeling of atmospheric convection in future studies.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to determine when this unconnected system could truly become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become entangled with the others if its cavity is highly occupied, provided that it is connected to another cavity with a specific type of quantum characteristic. Additionally, we examine various conditional operations on the unconnected system's atom, including measurements, interactions with a second atom, or a Jaynes-Cummings interaction with a new cavity, and how these operations affect the entanglement.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the (1+3)-dimensional Reissner-Nordstr\"om-Penrose non-linear charged AdS black hole. We examine the thermodynamics of this black hole within a shadow system, investigating how the radius and charge of the black hole influence the shadow profile. Additionally, we propose a non-linear generalization of the Chern-Simons term to incorporate a new scalar field, which results in a consistent theoretical framework. We then verify the effects of this term on shadow dynamics. Our findings related to the shadow profile are compared to previous research, with our non-linear approach demonstrating consistent results. We also explore the phase structures of this black hole in various non-linear theories of gravity, uncovering distinct phases based on the cosmological constant, along with the charge and scalar field. Our analysis reveals that the phase diagrams vary significantly with the choice of non-linear theory. We determine the conditions under which the black hole exists or disappears, which includes scenarios where it exits in a scalar-field-driven phase or a canonical phase characterized by the Reissner-Nordstr\"om solution. Our research thus provides comprehensive insights into the phase structures of nonlinear charged AdS black holes, along with the shadow profiles resulting from them.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and beginning of a quantum synchronization display distinct patterns of optical tomograms which can be recognized using a support vector machine. The accuracy of this result holds up even when the measurements are carried out with limited accuracy, significantly expanding the practical usefulness of this technique for detecting these important non-classical properties in a wide range of quantum systems.

360-degree virtual travel videos offer an immersive viewing experience but present challenges for navigation and orientation due to their comprehensive and sphere-shaped content. Researchers have proposed various methods to facilitate navigation by predicting the direction users will want to view next, but these tend to focus primarily on video features and overlook accompanying subtitles that provide vital information. In response, this study suggests a novel approach that combines both subtitle and video content to predict the desired viewing direction. Specifically, a viewport forecasting system is proposed that utilizes a deep neural network to analyze subtitles and a convolutional neural network to analyze video frames, then fuses their respective features to train a successful predictor model. Experiments conducted on real datasets reveal improved performance compared to existing methods that neglect subtitles, demonstrating the significance of considering both audio and visual elements in 360-degree virtual travel video navigation.

Tensor network techniques, which leverage the concept of a peudosparse pattern to capture complex systems, have been a successful tool for research in both statistical mechanics and quantum field theory. However, the method's precision comes at a cost of increased computational complexity. To balance precision and efficiency, the approach can be modified to ensure that the generators of the tensor network have a local character, which we demonstrate for both thermal equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium situations using the example of a massless scalar field. This leads to a new classification of the tensors based on their properties and behaviors, and enables the efficient calculation of both correlation functions and the Wightman function using a minimal number of operations.

Numerical methods for solving partial differential equations rely on the accuracy of approximations made in relation to the data, especially when dealing with hyperbolic equations. Despite the importance of assessing the accuracy of approximations, the existing literature primarily focuses on the stability and convergence of schemes rather than exploring the impact of approximations on solutions in relation to problem data. In contrast, the current study examines approximations in relation to data and classifies them as either oriented toward accuracy or oriented toward effectiveness, designing a framework to analyze the accuracy of schemes in relation to data. The development of this framework is demonstrated through the investigation of various approximation methods for hyperbolic equations, filling an existing gap in research on the subject.

Using a leading infrared divergence of PDF nonperturbative estimates, we investigate the impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole TMD gluon distribution at very small x. This analysis is relevant for future deep inelastic scattering experiments at high energies. We compare our results to existing datasets from the HERA era and forecast the accuracy required to detect infrared renormalons in future experiments, specifically the 50 GeV Z-boson case at the CLAS12 facility and 100 GeV case with a future deep inelastic scanner.

We present a theoretical model for a unique nanoarray made of rectangular holes in a gold film, which exhibits strong interaction between optical and magnetic fields. By manipulating the geometry of the holes, we can optimize this interaction and create a system where the magnetic field affects the optical behavior, specifically leading to a phenomenon called the Fano resonance. This resonance is highly sensitive to magnetic fields and could be used for very precise measurements. We also explored a 2D lattice made up of these nanoarrays and found that it can behave like a superfluid when it interacts with light, and this interaction can also cause the arrays to couple with each other in a specific pattern.

Recent advancements in neural network training have been successful, yet there's still a gap in understanding how neural networks train and mislead, particularly when biased data is used. Researchers have established methods for detecting and addressing bias, but they typically require access to training data and precise bias definitions, which isn't always the case. This study explores a different approach, inspired by a black-box decision-making framework, that enables neural networks to be effectively audited for bias without needing access to training data. In our experiment, we transferred knowledge from a neural network trained on a larger dataset to a smaller, more biased dataset, which allowed us to detect the underlying bias without difficulty. When we extended this approach to an unsupervised setting, we were able to discover valuable insights into how neural networks train and mislead, which couldn't be achieved through other audit techniques.

The study identifies possible signs of two rare occurrences, $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$, which have been hard to detect due to confusion with background from $B^0_s\to D^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$ decay patterns. The research uses 2019 and 2020 LHCb data, accumulating nearly 4000 $B^0_s\to D^0 K^0_S$ events after applying elimination criteria. For $B^0_s\to \bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0_S$ decays, evidence is found for these transitions with rates estimated at $1.0\times 10^{-7}$ for branching ratios and $0.19$ for decay ratio likelihood, both significantly beyond background expectations.

Given a module $R$ that is free from submodule multiplicities and a basis $B$ for this module, we develop a step-by-step procedure to construct the lattice of its submodules. Each submodule in this construction is associated with a set of defining polynomials, which can be used to identify isomorphic submodules. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the dimension of each submodule and calculate the index of each submodule within the parent module $R$. This process involves employing Grobner bases and other techniques from computational algebra, and it serves as a concrete realization of the abstract concept of building the lattice of submodules through exploration of the module's geometry.

Understanding how agents learn from each other through observation is vital in creating successful collaborative systems. In situations where agents have different areas of expertise, learning from each other is particularly useful, as it allows them to acquire new skills from each other. Currently, most co-learning methods require the expert agent to provide demonstrations of optimal actions for the task at hand, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. In this research, we explore a more adaptive approach called Co-Observation Learning (COL), where agents with varying levels of knowledge can learn from each other through observation alone. We develop a viable COL algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations. Our findings show that Co-Observation Learning leads to significant improvements in performance, especially in complex environments and with large knowledge gaps between agents.

We introduce PAC codes as a new code category that combines the error-correction capabilities of classical codes and the privacy preservation of quantum codes. Based on a threshold principle, we determine the required density for successful computation and estimate the error probability in a classical channel, also accounting for the accuracy of quantum operations. Furthermore, we outline specific protocols for measuring and analyzing PAC codes, including the evaluation of measurement outcomes and the calculation of quantum task success probabilities via the Euclidean norm and operator norm approaches.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation preprocessing can be effective in optimizing neural machine translation systems. Nonetheless, a significant issue with RL for NMT arises from the extensive action space resulting from the vocabulary size, which causes training to run into difficulties due in part to the vanishing exploration problem. Various approaches have been tried to expand the action space including repeatedly training the model, incorporating back translation, expanding the vocabulary, and trying different exploration techniques, yet most lead to suboptimal results. In order to address these challenges, a system called SANE-RL was developed, one that makes use of a unique combination of dense embeddings alongside exploration techniques, leading to notable improvements in benchmark metrics for NMT, specifically on WMT English to German, WMT English to French, and IWSLT English to Penguin translations.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly intriguing, and the study of spin baths is particularly engaging due to their straightforward implementation in the experimental domain. The combination of driving forces and open systems results in non-equilibrium steady states, whose characteristics rely on the solution of a stationary Schrödinger equation. The heat flow in the system or the entropy generation per period can be deduced from this solution. The change in the system's energy in relation to the driving strength, coupling to the bath, and periodic driving intensity can be quantified and has distinct features in different system configurations. The study includes a proposal for the experimental investigation of open quantum systems using a trapped ion.
We explore how certain recurring operators including differentiation and composition affect biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q, greater than 1, identifies two collections of rational numbers if it distinguishes between their inclusive and exclusive sums. In other words, there is a rational number 0 < n < 1 represented by one set but not the other. Our main contributions include determining sets of p/q values that can identify sets of size two, demonstrating that all such values lie between the square roots of 7 and 11, and cannot form a gap or consist of just one number. Additionally, we show that any set of p/q values capable of identifying pairs of size three requires at least three distinct components: a lower bound, an upper bound, and at least one non-identifiable p/q value.

MongoDB, a popular NoSQL database, offers a suite of transactions known as multi-document transactions. These transactions enable users to conduct multiple operations across different documents in a single, all-or-nothing transaction. As with SQL technologies, the complexity of these transactions exposes them to vulnerabilities, particularly data corruption and loss of consistency, should malicious actors exploit flaws in the system. The process of identifying these weaknesses involves examining the underlying logic of consistent replication, as the presence of malicious actors seeking to disrupt the system can lead to inconsistencies in data and ultimately breach transactional integrity. Our research into the public documentation of MongoDB reveals that the overall logic of consistent replication remains unclear, prompting us to hypothesize that there are undeclared assumptions underlying the architecture that could give rise to data corruption or breach transactional integrity. To test this hypothesis, we developed a precise model of MongoDB's consistent replication, including undeclared assumptions, which we used to investigate the validity of transactions and identify potential weaknesses in the system. Our analysis uncovered several weaknesses in MongoDB's transactional integrity, particularly with respect to distributed transactions, and highlights areas that could be improved to enhance the system's security.

Using the combinatorial definition of chromatic symmetric functions, we demonstrate that specific coefficients possess a desirable property, and in turn, gain insight into these functions'structural components. Specifically, it is shown that certain coefficients of the chromatic symmetric functions of partition (2,1) and (3,1) exhibit a particular characteristic and it is further implied that the symmetric functions in question are not readily expressible in a certain format.

Researchers from various fields including condensed matter, biology, finance, and astronomy have found intricate networks to be highly susceptible to catastrophic failures. Despite the diverse underlying geometry of these networks, certain patterns of node connections, such as loops of three and loops of four, have been found to provide superior stability compared to linear connections. Using a simple spin assembly model with triad-based interactions, we demonstrate the distinctive geometric signature of three-loop structures under magnetic field-induced spin reversal. We also established that assemblies consisting of loops of three and loops of four exhibit greater stability than those composed solely of loops of four, thereby requiring more rigorous conditions for spin reversal. Our findings can be applied across various fields, including magnetism, astronomy, and biology, where the geometry of networks affects dynamics and may influence phenomena like star formation and planet obstruction.

An analysis of solar wind data from the Parker Solar Probe mission reveals the existence of a variable solar breeze energy flow from 21 to 36 solar radii from the Sun. The research finds that the direction of this energy flow deviates significantly from radially, influencing its speed and pressure. It's believed this flow affects the Earth's magnetic field and solar wind dynamics. The study also finds that the energy flow's intensity and direction vary greatly over time, particularly in the solar breeze near the Sun's equator, and that it's correlated with solar wind acceleration, even when approaching a region known as the stagnation region.

To enhance communication, including bonding and conciliation, speech emotion recognition (SER) is being explored for potential uses in multiple areas. Despite significant progress made so far, existing models face two significant challenges. First, they require enormous amounts of labeled data for training, which can be difficult to obtain for a lot of practical applications. Second, they struggle to adapt to new domains quickly, which is a major limitation in environments where background noise and speakers are constantly changing. To overcome these obstacles, we've developed a practical SER system that's capable of adapting to new domains quickly. This system uses a combination of domain adaptation and agent-based deep reinforcement learning techniques to improve the performance of emotion recognition within a small amount of labeled data and multiple unnamed speech emotions. We gathered two sets of data for the experiment: one for training and another for testing. The training data included 3,000 recorded voices from 10 listeners with 7 emotion classifications, and the testing data consisted of 4,000 recorded voices from a distinct group of 15 listeners with the same 7 emotion classifications. Notably, the speakers in the testing group spoke differently than those in the training group. According to the results, the proposed system significantly improved performance compared to the standard model, with 72% domain adaptation accuracy and an emotional recognition rate of 85%.

Researchers studying high-energy particle physics have a strong interest in enterring an extremely high-density state deep within dense matter, yet this density is difficult to achieve in laboratory settings. However, such conditions can be easily created in the heart of dense matter through a robust shock wave induced by a high-power laser, and in a spherical cavity it can be maintained for a longer duration. A pair of exact solutions to the Einstein--Friedmann equations has been applied to model a dense matter model with a spherical cavity, yielding information on the pressure and density at its core. Furthermore, we examine the effects of various parameters such as the initial mass-energy density, the properties of a particular field that causes structure to form, and the rate at which the cosmos is expanding, on the state of dense matter.

Using $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ data, an investigation of the QCD approach to determine the $b$ quark mass is conducted, alternative methods of calculation are examined, and the consistency of the data with theoretical predictions is tested. Leveraging a 0.305 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ luminosity of $10.48 \text{ TeV}$ $s$-channel $B_s^0$ data, obtained at LHCb, a new estimate of the $b$ quark mass is calculated with reduced uncertainty, and the validity of the heavy quark expansion is validated until a dimensionless energy $\bar{\tau} \approx 0.25$.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property.

A persistent pattern of sound occurs when an adhesive tape with periodic attachments is pulled at a steady speed. Despite being seemingly random, the time intervals between the attachments follow a pattern of deviation from exponential distribution. In contrast to previous interpretations suggesting connections to fractional dynamics or power-law distributions, our findings reveal that the distribution of time intervals can be non-exponentially periodic, yet still lead to the appearance of fractional dynamics in the sound cracks. We demonstrate that the distribution of time intervals can be approximated as a gamma distribution, which results in a beta distribution of time intervals. This explains the observed periodic fluctuations in the distribution of time intervals and provides a straightforward explanation for the adhesive tape's behavior.

In this research, we incorporate non-abelian aether-like terms within the Faddeev-Slavov framework for a polynomial gauge theory, expanding on a previous study by Dick and Trambore-Weisberg from 1978. Non-abelian aether-like terms, which involve covariant derivatives, have no impact on physical content but affect temperature and momentum behavior of poles. Leveraging heat kernel coefficients, we evaluate non-abelian aether-like counterterms for general gauge theories, determining their coefficients under both the 't Hooft and 't Hooft-Lee schemes. For a specific scalar self-coupled theory, we directly compute these counterterms. Additionally, we provide non-abelian aether-like counterterms for a class of massless scalar fields with arbitrary symmetry properties.

This study develops a comprehensive framework for assessing option-based collateral requirements, considering the costs of hedging and refreshing liquidity. Unlike previous approaches, which rely on numerical methods to solve this issue, our research utilizes an analytical technique to provide a precise formula for estimating the expected cost of hedging one unit of delta. This expression, coupled with the price of a binary option, enables the calculation of the expected shortfall of a portfolio due to hedging failures. Our results involve constructing a specific binary option price model, which is subsequently applied to investigate large variety of static options collateral requirements. Dynamic scenarios are tackled by developing a new change-of-variables theorem to solve a related stochastic partial differential equation.

A dynamic model of social mobility explores how economic opportunities are allocated across generations. In a closed system with no population growth, a perfect meritocracy ensures that each generation inherits exactly what its members are worthy of. However, introducing a gap between descriptive and prescriptive fairness creates inequality when considering how worth relates to inheritance. When the relationship between descriptive and prescriptive worth isn't linear, a small population growth rate can mitigate this inequality and make the system more fair, although only in a limited sense. A linear relationship, on the other hand, requires a specific population growth rate to maintain fairness, depending on how worth is calculated. Not all reference standards will achieve this balance, as those that prioritize earlier generations' welfare won't see improved fairness, even with large growth rates.

A method called "brightness scans" reduces the number of beam scans required to determine the shape and orientation of a non-uniform electron beam. By measuring the intensity of a a rectangular beam at two points, rather than multiple scans along different lines, this approach determines the beam's position, orientation, and curvature within a limited area. Brightness scans are particularly beneficial for systems that move slowly and where it takes a long time to gather data, such as in photoelectron microscopy. This research demonstrates the utility of brightness scans in monitoring the stability of an electron beam over time, comparing the advantages of continuous versus discrete scanning strategies.

This paper presents a new optimization framework for dealing with malicious users in a cooperative setting, characterized by the presence of assaultive users who benefit from the social welfare decrease and the existence of private data with users that follow a subgradient rule based on their private information. In this context, we develop the Quantized and Distributed Subgradient Improvement (QDSI) algorithm, which incorporates quantization and gradient updating components to minimize friction in information exchange. We also establish the convergence of the QDSI algorithm under the assumption that the set of honest users forms a beta-mixing time series with finite variance. Additionally, we examine the impact of malicious users and data privacy on the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its resilience in various scenarios, and providing specific conditions under which the number of assaultive users affects the algorithm's convergence rate.

The study of the cosmic microwave background is a fundamental area in astronomy, and the development of highly sensitive experiments is crucial for tackling fundamental problems in the cosmos. However, the sheer amount of data these experiments produce requires highly advanced analysis techniques and significant computational resources. This paper introduces a new open-source software tool called s4cmb, an extension to the existing s4psd package, which generates simulated data streams in the time domain representing signals from cosmic microwave background telescopes. The tool can produce multiple simulated streams from different detectors with varied frequencies and beam patterns, and it includes realistic simulations of instrumental effects such as non-linearities, systematic gains, and correlated noise. Furthermore, the tool offers efficient storage of simulated data in a compact and accessible format, facilitating rapid retrieval of specific time intervals and frequency bands. The tool is highly compatible with existing data analysis software, specifically designed to handle time domain signals, and it includes example use cases for simulating and aligning multiple detector signals, as well as for applying data quality cuts based on simulated attributes.

In the context of word arrangement tasks, pre-trained linguistic models can be both beneficial and distracting. While they possess extensive linguistic knowledge, their training data also includes noisy information from translation tasks, such as sentence structures commonly seen in NMT datasets. These structures are typically already assumed to be correct and may lead to biased results in tasks like word arrangement where multiple possible structures exist and must be evaluated. Our analysis highlights the intricate relationship between the underlying architecture of pre-trained models and their performance in word arrangement tasks, demonstrating that the distribution of dependency relationships reflected in the training data influences performance. We also examine the effect of different module combinations on the performance of BART and find that only a subset of the model is necessary to achieve high scores in word arrangement tasks. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings for approaches to evaluating and using pre-trained models in tasks that require the exploration of complex syntactic structures.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic deepfake media poses a substantial challenge to traditional fact-checking methods. Deepfake technology's rapid evolution necessitates a versatile and highly effective deepfake detection system. Inspired by the success of cross-network training in enhancing the robustness of deepfake detection models, this research introduces a novel framework called the MD-CSDNetwork, a multi-domain cross-sewn network designed to counter deepfake misinformation. The proposed framework redefines cross-network training by incorporating a twisting technique that prevents overreliance on source-domain information. This results in a highly generalizable model with superior performance in both source and target domains. Experimental evaluations on widely used deepfake detection datasets demonstrate the superiority of the MD-CSDNetwork approach.

In 1911, Menger introduced the term "abstract space" to describe a pair $A, \mathcal{C}$ where $A$ is a set and $\mathcal{C}$ is a collection of subsets of $A$ with specific properties, including being closed under finite intersection. Building upon this concept, Menger developed the theory of angle spaces, using the standard metric to define distances between subspaces. Two notable problems stood out in his work: (1) whether the unit angle in a space can be realized as the intersection of finitely many closed subspaces, and (2) whether the distance between two subspaces is equal to the cosine of the angle between them. In this paper, we resolve these two problems that have been unanswered since their initial presentation over a century ago.

We establish the primality of certain rank reductions in number theory fields. To illustrate this concept, consider the Diophantine equation described by the polynomial $f(y)^2 - ax^3 - bx^2 - cx - d = 0$. For this equation, assuming $a, b, c, d$ are relatively prime and belong to $\mathbb Q$, the rank of its integer solutions can be determined. Specifically, if the discriminant $\Delta$ of the polynomial $f(y)$ is a square-free integer and its associated Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ has a specific structure, the rank of its integer solutions is conditioned on the primality of $\Delta$. Moreover, this condition leads to constraints on the rank of the associated Jacobian variety and its connection to the arithmetic of its defining polynomial.

We introduce the concept of cluster characters for the represetning theory of quantum groups, demonstrating they form an additive basis for the ring of functions on the dual torus. This character matches the ring's extremal module when equipped with a natural poset structure, specifically, it corresponds to the extreme point of a polytope whose vertices are computed by a variant of Knuth's, using the fundamental involutions of the Weyl group. This connection between the extremal initial cluster and the extremal final cluster yields a combinatorial interpretation of the Coxeter numbers within the structure of the Weyl group.

Pyramid scams are a well-known investment deception where members earn refunds from newer participants to climb the rank and collect significant payouts. Researchers have analyzed the underlying structure of a high-tech pyramid scam called Forsage, which uses cryptocurrency smart contracts. By developing a referral network map based on public data, our study reveals the intricate design of this scheme and how it affects those involved in it. Specifically, our work examines the structure's impact on participants by tracking rankings, earnings, and contract usage. Unlike traditional pyramid scams, Forsage's architecture remains unaltered as it spreads, given its smart contract nature. This leads to a critical period before mass adoption where participants can earn high returns, only to decline as the scheme reaches its equilibrium state. Our findings are relevant to multiple fields, including cryptography, finance, and sociology, where the incidence of scams is a persistent problem.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters is being investigated to clarify the list of confirmed clusters. Although most clusters have a well-established history, some prospects with uncertain status have emerged, particularly in the galaxy's bulge region. The number of prospects has been reduced from over a hundred to under a hundred based on the analysis of the most reliable criteria including spatial distribution, color, and luminosity. The research focuses on the 19 most uncertain prospects among newly discovered clusters in the galaxy's bulge and determines that only two clusters are likely new ones; the remaining 17 clusters can be explained by concentrating light on the galaxy's bulge rather than being distant objects.

In this context, we explore a new type of holographic tensor network, which we call Hyper-Invariant MERA (iMERA), and identify its distinguishing features through a comprehensive analysis of its architecture. A key advantage of iMERA networks lies in their ability to efficiently manage various invariant total entropy measures, effectively capturing regional characteristics with precision. Additionally, we find that these networks can replicate certain holographic duality relationships previously observed in regular MERA constructions. Furthermore, we subscribe to a notion that holographic duality itself can be viewed as a theory of error correction, and in support of this idea, we establish that the entropy associated with a particular region in iMERA constructions matches the result obtained via a holographic duality principle applied to that same region. Notably, this error-correcting scenario is characterized by a power-law distance between the code's generation region and the site from which the code is extracted, and we demonstrate that networks defined by a specific set of tensor transformations are capable of achieving this law through a process of renormalization. Moreover, we demonstrate that both the conformal iMERA and the entanglement-renormalization-defined iMERA constructions map to the same physical system when using the same set of tensor transformations, and we append an informal discussion on the relationship between these constructions and the features of holographic duality error correction.

Understanding and predicting complex business processes involve analyzing and interpreting time-series data with multiple components. Deep learning methods such as graph-based models, recurrent neural networks, and neural network-based time series forecasting have been successful in processing and predicting business processes. However, there are limited research on the comparison of deep learning techniques for process-related data. In contrast to traditional methods of time-series analysis, deep learning techniques offer a more intuitive understanding of internal process variables. Yet, there is little information available on the comparison of these techniques or the impact of their components on predictive models. Furthermore, there is a lack of research on the comparison of deep learning techniques versus traditional time-series analysis methods. In contrast to the prevalent focus on predictive performance, there is little examination of the comparison of these techniques or the impact of their components on predictive models. In this work, we compare graph-based models to recurrent neural networks and neural network-based time series forecasting techniques for predicting complex business processes. My research reveals significant differences in the characteristics of deep learning techniques and their components, which in turn affect the predictive performance. Furthermore, I found that there is little distinction between the predictive performance of traditional time-series analysis methods and the deep learning techniques examined. My research used business process datasets extracted from actual data, which were represented as multi-level time-series data.

We investigate key properties of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, identifying their characteristic features that distinguish them from other spaces. It is demonstrated that standard applications of Toeplitz operators rely on specific, non-default assumptions about the character of these spaces.

A novel approach is taken to analyze the UV behavior of the massive stellar flare from the giant flare star AD Leo in 1985, utilizing a computational model rather than observational data. The model, incorporating observations from different wavelengths, accurately replicates the continuing evolution of the stellar surface and the surrounding space environment. The simulated near-ultraviolet continuum for this event is specifically examined, with the goal of better understanding the post-eruption activity on flare stars in the UV spectrum.

Neural network-based point cloud representation techniques often incorporate the spatial structure of input points through local connection graphs. These methods typically employ a consistent all-to-all connection pattern, which can be limiting due to the fixed structure. In contrast, many real-world applications involve objects with complex, irregular shapes that lack all-to-all connectivity.
